input.question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.
input.ground_truth: Because a breakthrough towards a cure is just one brick in the road, but it's what gets highly touted by the media because it's easy to point out. A team of scientists working in lab conditions come up with something promising and release their findings. Someone in the media sees this paper and turns "Disease has possible vulnerability!" and turns it into "CURE IS IMMINENT!!!1!" What they don't say is that it will take another few years of research, plus another few years of study, then another few years to create a human-safe cure (doesn't do anyone any good to cure the disease if it kills the patient as well), and then a few more years to figure out how to produce it at profitable levels.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, imagine you are playing with your building blocks. You build a really tall tower, but sometimes it falls down before you can show it to your friends. Scientists are like that when they try to make new medicines.

They try and try to build something that will help people feel better, like a magic medicine. But making a real medicine is super, super hard. Most of the time, their first tries don’t work, or maybe they help a little but not enough. It’s like building a tower that almost stands up, but not quite.

So, scientists keep trying new ideas, and that’s why you hear about lots of new things in the news. But before a new medicine can help everyone, it has to be checked many times to make sure it really works and is safe. That takes a long, long time. So even though there are lots of new ideas, only a few of them become real cures that help people for sure.
